title: Judge Says Trump’s Mail-In Voting Rules Can Stay—For Now
summary: Have you ever mailed a letter and wondered how it gets to the right place? Now imagine if the government said only certain people could get their ballots by mail. That’s what President Trump’s new order wants to do. But a judge just said it’s too early to block it. On Thursday, Judge Carl Nichols ruled that Trump’s order can stay for now. The order tells the Postal Service to only deliver mail-in ballots to people on special lists. It also wants Homeland Security and Social Security to make lists of adult U.S. citizens for each state. But here’s the catch: none of this has happened yet. The judge said since the rules aren’t in place, there’s nothing to stop right now. Many Democrats and voting rights groups are upset. They say the order is really about making it harder for some people to vote. Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer called it “voter suppression, plain and simple.” They argue that the Constitution gives states and Congress—not the president—the power to set election rules. Trump says he’s trying to stop noncitizens from voting, but studies show that almost never happens. The fight isn’t over. Another judge in Boston might decide soon, and the groups can come back to court if the rules actually start. So for now, the mail-in voting debate is still in the mailbox.
why_it_matters: This matters because someday you’ll be able to vote, and the rules about how you vote could affect whether your voice counts.

background_read: In the United States, each state runs its own elections, following rules set by state governments and Congress.
Mail-in voting, also called absentee voting, became very popular during the COVID-19 pandemic.
President Donald Trump (the U.S. president since 2025) has often claimed that mail-in voting leads to fraud, but experts say it is very safe.
Article_Structure: WHO: Judge Carl Nichols, President Trump, Democrats, Chuck Schumer
WHAT: Trump’s order about mail-in ballots was allowed to stay because no rules have been made yet
WHERE: In the United States (a federal court in Washington, D.C.)
WHY: The judge said there’s nothing to block; the fight is over voting rights and who sets election rules

perspectives.description: Trump says the order is needed to make elections secure and stop noncitizens from voting, which he believes protects fairness.
Democrats and voting rights groups say the order is really about making it harder for some Americans, especially certain groups, to vote.
Legal experts say the Constitution gives election powers to states and Congress, so the court will have to decide if the president can change voting rules.
